Controllers - Lightguns - Konami Justifier/Hyperblaster (IRQ10)
---------------------------------------------------------------

Overall IRQ10-Based Lightgun Access
  Send  01h 42h 00h x0h 00h
  Reply HiZ 31h 5Ah buttons
The purpose of the "x0h" byte is probably to enable IRQ10 (00h=off, 10h=on),
this would allow to access more than one lightgun (with only one per frame
having the IRQ enabled).

Standard IRQ10-based Lightguns (Konami)
The Controller Data simply consists of the ID and buttons states:
  __Halfword 0 (Controller Info)___________________
  0-15  Controller Info  (5A31h=Konami Lightgun; Timer/IRQ10 type)
  __Halfword 1 (Buttons)
  0-2   Not used                 (All bits always 1)
  3     Start Button (Left Side) (0=Pressed, 1=Released)  ;aka Joypad Start
  4-13  Not used                 (All bits always 1)
  14    Back Button  (Rear End)  (0=Pressed, 1=Released)  ;aka Joypad X-Button
  15    Trigger Button           (0=Pressed, 1=Released)  ;aka Joypad []-Button
The coordinates aren't part of the controller data, instead they must be read
from Timer 0 and 1 upon receiving IRQ10 (see IRQ10 Notes below).

     __                 ______ _
   _|__\_______________/  ___ \ \   Konami Justifier/Hyperblaster (light green)
  |   _______________ __ /   \ \ \
  |__|   _ _ _ _     |==|    O| \O\ .... Back Button (Rear End)
     |__:_:_:_:_:__  |___\__ /  ( (
                   |_|  ) \  :   \ \
      Trigger ......  \___/| :...|.|.... Start Button (Left Side)

Konami IRQ10 Notes
The PSX does have a lightgun input (Pin 8 of the controller), but, Sony did
apparently "forget" to latch the current cathode ray beam coordinates by
hardware when sensing the lightgun signal (quite strange, since that'd be a
simple, inexpensive, and very obvious feature for a gaming console).
Instead, the lightgun signal triggers IRQ10, and the interrupt handler is
intended to "latch" the coordinates by software (by reading Timer 0 and 1
values, which must configured to be synchronized with the GPU).
That method requires IRQ handling to be properly implemented in software
(basically, IRQs should not be disabled for longer periods, and DMA transfers
should not block the bus for longer periods). In practice, most programmers
probably don't realize how to do that, to the worst, Sony seems to have
delivered a slightly bugged library (libgun) to developers.
For details on Timers, see:
--> Timers
In some consoles, IRQ10 seems to be routed through a Secondary IRQ Controller,
see:
--> EXP2 DTL-H2000 I/O Ports

IRQ10 Priority
For processing IRQ10 as soon as possible, it should be assigned higher priority
than all other IRQs (ie. when using the SysEnqIntRP BIOS function, it should be
the first/newest element in priority chain 0). The libgun stuff assigns an even
higher priority by patching the BIOS exception handler, causing IRQ10 to be
processed shortly before processing the priority chains (the resulting IRQ
priority isn't actually higher as when using 1st element of chain 0; the main
difference is that it skips some time consuming code which pushes registers
R4..R30). For details on that patch, see:
--> BIOS Patches
Even if IRQ10 has highest priority, execution of (older) other IRQs may cause a
new IRQ10 to be executed delayed (because IRQs are disabled during IRQ
handling), to avoid that problem: Best don't enable any other IRQs except IRQ0
and IRQ10, or, if you need other IRQs, best have them enabled only during
Vblank (there are no scanlines drawn during vblank, so IRQ10 should never
trigger during that period). DMAs might also slow down IRQ execution, so best
use them only during Vblank, too.

IRQ10 Timer Reading
To read the current timer values the IRQ10 handler would be required to be
called <immediately> after receiving the IRQ10 signal, which is more or less
impossible; if the main program is trying to read a mul/div/gte result while
the mul/div/gte operation is still busy may stop the CPU for some dozens of
clock cycles, and active DMA transfers or cache hits and misses in the IRQ
handler may cause different timings, moreover, timings may become completely
different if IRQs are disabled (eg. while another IRQ is processed).
However, IRQ10 does also get triggered in the next some scanlines, so the first
IRQ10 is used only as a notification that the CPU should watch out for further
IRQ10's. Ie. the IRQ10 handler should disable all DMAs, acknowledge IRQ10, and
then enter a waitloop that waits for the IRQ10 bit in I_STAT to become set
again (or abort if a timeout occurs) and then read the timers, reportedly like
so:
  IF NTSC then X=(Timer0-140)*0.198166, Y=Timer1
  IF PAL  then X=(Timer0-140)*0.196358, Y=Timer1
No idea why PAL/NTSC should use different factors, that factors are looking
quite silly/bugged, theoretically, the pixel-to-clock ratio should be the
exactly same for PAL and NTSC...?
Mind that reading Timer values in Dotclock/Hblank mode is unstable, for Timer1
this can be fixed by the read-retry method, for Timer0 this could be done too,
but one would need to subtract the retry-time to get a correct coordinate;
alternately Timer0 can run at system clock (which doesn't require read-retry),
but it must be then converted to video clock (mul 11, div 7), and then from
video clock to dot clock (eg. div 8 for 320-pixel mode).
Above can be repeated for the next some scanlines (allowing to take the medium
values as result, and/or to eliminate faulty values which are much bigger or
smaller than the other values). Once when you have collected enough values,
disable IRQ10, so it won't trigger on further scanlines within the current
frame.

IRQ10 Bugs
BUG: The "libgun" library doesn't acknowledge the old IRQ10 <immediately>
before waiting for a new IRQ10, so the timer values after sensing the new IRQ10
are somewhat random (especially for the first processed scanline) (the library
allows to read further IRQ10's in further scanlines, which return more stable
results).
No idea how many times IRQ10 gets typically repeated? Sporting Clays allocates
a buffer for up to 20 scanlines (which would cause pretty much of a slowdown
since the CPU is just waiting during that period) (nethertheless, the game uses
only the first timer values, ie. the bugged libgun-random values).

Unknown if/how two-player games (with 2 lightguns) are working with the IRQ10
method... if IRQ10 is generated ONLY after pressing the trigger button, then it
may work, unless both players have Trigger pressed at the same time... and,
maybe one can enable/disable the lightguns by whatever commmand being sent to
the controller (presumably that "x0h" byte, see above), so that gun 1 generates
IRQ10 only in each second frame, and gun 2 only in each other frame...?

See also
--> Pinouts - Component List and Chipset Pin-Outs for Konami Lightgun, RU012

Controllers - Configuration Commands
------------------------------------

Some controllers can be switched from Normal Mode to Config Mode. The Config
Mode was invented for activating the 2nd rumble motor in SCPH-1200 analog
joypads. Additionally, the Config commands can switch between analog/digital
inputs (without needing to manually press the Analog button), activate more
analog inputs (on Dualshock2), and read some type/status bytes.

Normal Mode
  42h "B" Read Buttons (and analog inputs when in analog mode)
  43h "C" Enter/Exit Configuration Mode (stay normal, or enter)
Transfer length in Normal Mode is 5 bytes (Digital mode), or 9 bytes (Analog
mode), or up to 21 bytes (Dualshock2).

Configuration Mode
  40h "@" Unused, or Dualshock2: Get/Set ButtonAttr?
  41h "A" Unused, or Dualshock2: Get Reply Capabilities
  42h "B" Read Buttons AND analog inputs (even when in digital mode)
  43h "C" Enter/Exit Configuration Mode (stay config, or exit)
  44h "D" Set LED State (analog mode on/off)
  45h "E" Get LED State (and Type/constants)
  46h "F" Get Variable Response A (depending on incoming bit) ("PadInfoAct")
  47h "G" Get whatever values (response HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 02h 00h 01h 00h)
  48h "H" Unknown             (response HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 00h 00h 01h 00h)
  49h "I" Unused
  4Ah "J" Unused
  4Bh "K" Unused (or MORE bytes from "PadInfoComb")
  4Ch "L" Get Variable Response B (depending on incoming bit) (PadInfoMode)
  4Dh "M" Get/Set RumbleProtocol
  4Eh "N" Unused
  4Fh "O" Unused, or Dualshock2: Set ReplyProtocol
Transfer length in Config Mode is always 9 bytes.

 ____________________________ Normal Mode Commands ____________________________

Normal Mode - Command 42h "B" - Read Buttons (and analog inputs when enabled)
  Send  01h 42h 00h xx  yy  (00h 00h 00h 00h) (...)
  Reply HiZ id  5Ah buttons ( analog-inputs ) (dualshock2 buttons...)
The normal read command, see Standard Controller chapter for details on buttons
and analog inputs. The xx/yy bytes have effect only if rumble is unlocked; use
Command 43h to enter config mode, and Command 4Dh to unlock rumble. Command 4Dh
has billions of combinations, among others allowing to unlock only one of the
two motors, and to exchange the xx/yy bytes, however, with the default values,
xx/yy are assigned like so:
  yy.bit0-7 ---> Left/Large Motor M1 (analog slow/fast) (00h=stop, FFh=fastest)
  xx.bit0   ---> Right/small Motor M2 (digital on/off)  (0=off, 1=on)
The Left/Large motor starts spinning at circa min=50h..60h, and, once when
started keeps spinning downto circa min=38h. The exact motor start boundary
depends on the current position of the weight (if it's at the "falling" side,
then gravity helps starting), and also depends on external movements (eg. it
helps if the user or the other rumble motor is shaking the controller), and may
also vary from controller to controller, and may also depend on the room
temperature, dirty or worn-out mechanics, etc.

Normal Mode - Command 43h "C" - Enter/Exit Configuration Mode
  Send  01h 43h 00h xx  00h (zero padded...)   (...)
  Reply HiZ id  5Ah buttons (analog inputs...) (dualshock2 buttons...)
When issuing command 43h from inside normal mode, the response is same as for
command 42h (button data) (and analog inputs when in analog mode) (but without
M1 and M2 parameters). While in config mode, the ID bytes are always "F3h 5Ah"
(instead of the normal analog/digital ID bytes).
  xx=00h Stay in Normal mode
  xx=01h Enter Configuration mode
Caution: Additionally to activating configuration commands, entering config
mode does also activate a Watchdog Timer which does reset the controller if
there's been no communication for about 1 second or so. The watchdog timer
remains active even when returning to normal mode via Exit Config command. The
reset does disable and lock rumble motors, and switches the controller to
Digital Mode (with LED=off, and analog inputs disabled). To prevent this, be
sure to keep issuing joypad reads even when not needing user input (eg. while
loading data from CDROM).
Caution 2: A similar reset occurs when the user pushes the Analog button; this
is causing rumble motors to be stopped and locked, and of course, the
analog/digital state gets changed.
Caution 3: If config commands were used, and the user does then push the analog
button, then the 5Ah-byte gets replaced by 00h (ie. responses change from "HiZ
id 5Ah ..." to "HiZ id 00h ...").

 ____________________________ Config Mode Commands ____________________________

Config Mode - Command 42h "B" - Read Buttons AND analog inputs
  Send  01h 42h 00h M2  M1  00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah buttons  analog-inputs
Same as command 42h in normal mode, but with forced analog response (ie. analog
inputs and L3/R3 buttons are returned even in Digital Mode with LED=Off).

Config Mode - Command 43h "C" - Enter/Exit Configuration Mode
  Send  01h 43h 00h xx  00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
Equivalent to command 43h in normal mode, but returning 00h bytes rather than
button data, can be used to return to normal mode.
  xx=00h Enter Normal mode (Exit Configuration mode)
  xx=01h Stay in Configuration mode
Back in normal mode, the rumble motors (if they were enabled) can be controlled
with normal command 42h.

Config Mode - Command 44h "D" - Set LED State (analog mode on/off)
Note: This is called PadSetMainMode in official docs.
  Send  01h 44h 00h Led Key 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h Err 00h 00h 00h
The Led byte can be:
  When Led=00h      --> Digital mode, with LED=Off
  When Led=01h      --> Analog mode, with LED=On/red
  When Led=02h..FFh --> Ignored (and, in case of dualshock2: set Err=FFh)
The Key byte can be:
  When Key=00h..02h --> Unlock (allow user to push Analog button)
  When Key=03h      --> Lock (stay in current mode, ignore Analog button)
  When Key=04h..FFh --> Acts same as (Key AND 03h)
The Err byte is usually 00h (except, Dualshock2 sets Err=FFh upon Led=02h..FFh;
older PSX/PSone controllers don't do that).

Config Mode - Command 45h "E" - Get LED State (and Type/constants)
  Send  01h 45h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah Typ Num Led Act Com 00h
Returns several interesting bytes:
  Typ: Controller Type (01h=PSX/Analog Pad, 03h=PS2/Dualshock2)
  Num: Number of Modes                  (usually 02h) (for cmd 4Ch)
  Led: Current Mode (usually 00h=Digital/LedOff, 01h=Analog/LedRed)
  Act: Number of Actuators (aka motors) (usually 02h) (for cmd 46h)
  Com: Number of Combiner Lists         (usually 01h) (for cmd 47h)

Config Mode - Command 46h "F" - Get Variable Response A ("PadInfoAct")
  Send  01h 46h 00h ii  00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h Fnc Sub Siz Pwr
This is called PadInfoAct in official docs, ii is the actuator (aka motor).
The meaning of the return values is:
  Fnc  InfoActFunc  Function type (01h=Continuous-rotation vibration)
  Sub  InfoActSub   Sub-type (rotation-speed when Fnc=01h: 1=Low, 2=High)
  Siz  InfoActSize  Parameter data length
                     (0: 1 bit (ON/OFF only), 1 or greater: number of bytes)
  Pwr  InfoActCurr  Maximum current drain (0Ah=Small, 14h=Big)
Return values are usually:
  When ii=00h   --> returns Fnc,Sub,Siz,Pwr = 01h,02h,00h,0ah  ;small motor
  When ii=01h   --> returns Fnc,Sub,Siz,Pwr = 01h,01h,01h,14h  ;big motor
  When ii=Other --> returns Fnc,Sub,Siz,Pwr = all zeroes
The last response byte contains the 7.5V supply current drain (10 or 20 units).
Whereas, Sony insists that controllers should never exceed 60 units (eg. when
having more than 2 joypads connected to multitaps).

Config Mode - Command 47h "G" - Get whatever values ("PadInfoComb")
  Send  01h 47h 00h ii  00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 02h 00h 01h 00h
When ii=00h --> returns 02h 00h 01h 00h as shown above
   ii  = list number
   02h = num entries in selected list?
   00h,01h = entries in that list? (combining actuator 00h and 01h is allowed)
Otherwise --> returns zeroes

Config Mode - Command 4Ch "L" - Get Variable Response B (PadInfoMode)
Note: This is called PadInfoMode in official docs. (?)
  Send  01h 4Ch 00h ii  00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h cc  dd  00h 00h
When ii=00h --> returns cc,dd=00h,04h  ;ExID=4  ;for 5A41h = Digital Pad mode?
When ii=01h --> returns cc,dd=00h,07h  ;ExID=7  ;for 5A73h = Analog Pad mode?
Otherwise --> returns cc,dd=00h,00h.

Config Mode - Command 48h "H" - Unknown
  Send  01h 48h 00h ii  00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 00h 00h ee  00h
When ii=00h..01h --> returns ee=01h.
Otherwise --> returns ee=00h.
Purpose unknown. The command does not seem to be used by any games.

Config Mode - Command 4Dh "M" - Get/Set RumbleProtocol
--> Controllers - Vibration/Rumble Control

Config Mode - Command 40h "@" Dualshock2: Get/Set ButtonAttr?
Config Mode - Command 41h "A" Dualshock2: Get Reply Capabilities
Config Mode - Command 4Fh "O" Dualshock2: Set ReplyProtocol
--> Controllers - Analog Buttons (Dualshock2)

Config Mode - Command 49h "I" - Unused
Config Mode - Command 4Ah "J" - Unused
Config Mode - Command 4Bh "K" - Unused (or MORE bytes from "PadInfoComb")
Config Mode - Command 4Eh "N" - Unused
Config Mode - Command 40h "@" - Unused (except, used by Dualshock2)
Config Mode - Command 41h "A" - Unused (except, used by Dualshock2)
Config Mode - Command 4Fh "O" - Unused (except, used by Dualshock2)
  Send  01h 4xh 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
These commands do return a bunch of 00h bytes. These commands do not seem to be
used by any games (apart from the Dualshock2 commands being used by Dualshock2
games).

Note
Something called "Guitar Hero controller" does reportedly also support Config
commands. Unknown if that thing does have the same inputs & rumble motors as
normal analog PSX joypads, and if it does return special type values.

Controllers - Vibration/Rumble Control
--------------------------------------

Rumble (aka "Vibration Function") is basically controlled by two previously
unused bytes of the standard controller Read command.
There are two methods to control the rumble motors, the old method is very
simple (but supports only one motor), the new method envolves a bunch of new
configuration commands (and supports two motors).
  SCPH-1150  DualAnalog Pad with 1 motor                  ;-old rumble method
  SCPH-1200  DualAnalog Pad with 2 motors, PSX-design     ;\new rumble method
  SCPH-110   DualAnalog Pad with 2 motors, PSone-design   ;/
  SCPH-10010 DualAnalog Pad with 2 motors, PS2/Dualshock2 ;-plus analog buttons
  Blaze Scorpion Lightgun with rumble      ;\unknow how to control rumble
  Fishing controllers with rumble          ;/
  SCPH-1180 Analog Pad without rumble      ;\unknow if there're config commands
  SCPH-1110 Analog Stick without rumble    ;/for analog mode (probably not)

 _________________________________ Old Method _________________________________

Old Method, one motor, no config commands (SCPH-1150, SCPH-1200, SCPH-110)
The SCPH-1150 doesn't support any special config commands, instead, rumble is
solely done via the normal joypad read command:
  Send  01h 42h 00h xx  yy  (00h 00h 00h 00h)
  Reply HiZ id  5Ah buttons ( analog-inputs )
The rumble motor is simply controlled by three bits in the xx/yy bytes:
  xx --> must be 40h..7Fh            (ie. bit7=0, bit6=1) ;\switches motor on
  yy --> must be 01h,03h,...,FDh,FFh (ie. bit0=1)         ;/
The motor control is digital on/off (no analog slow/fast), recommended values
would be yyxx=0140h=on, and yyxx=0000h=off.
LED state is don't care (rumble works with led OFF, RED, and GREEN). In absence
of config commands, the LED can be controlled only manually (via Analog
button), the current LED state is implied in the controller "id" byte.
For backwards compatibility, the above old method does also work on SCPH-1200
and SCPH-110 (for controlling the right/small motor), alternately those newer
pads can use the config commands (for gaining access to both motors).

 _________________________________ New Method _________________________________

New Method, two motors, with config commands (SCPH-1200, SCPH-110)
For using the new rumble method, one must unlock the new rumble mode, for that
purpose Sony has invented a "slightly" overcomplicated protocol with not less
than 16 new commands (the rumble relevant commands are 43h and 4Dh, also,
command 44h may be useful for activating analog inputs by software, and, once
when rumble is unlocked, command 42h is used to control the rumble motors;
using data from "PadSetAct" function). Anyways, here's the full command set...
--> Controllers - Configuration Commands
And, the rumble-specific config command is described below...

Config Mode - Command 4Dh "M" - Get/Set RumbleProtocol
This is called "PadSetActAlign" in official docs.
  Send  01h 4Dh 00h aa  bb  cc  dd  ee  ff     ;<-- set NEW aa..ff values
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah aa  bb  cc  dd  ee  ff     ;<-- returns OLD aa..ff values
Bytes aa,bb,cc,dd,ee,ff control the meaning of the 4th,5th,6th,7th,8th,9th
command byte in the controller read command (Command 42h).
  00h      = Map Right/small Motor (Motor M2) to bit0 of this byte
  01h      = Map Left/Large Motor (Motor M1) to bit0-7 of this byte
  02h..FEh = Unknown (can be mapped, maybe for extra motors/outputs)
  FFh      = Map nothing to this byte
In practice, one would usually send either one of these command/values:
  Send  01h 4Dh 00h 00h 01h FFh FFh FFh FFh    ;enable new method (two motors)
  Send  01h 4Dh 00h FFh FFh FFh FFh FFh FFh    ;disable motor control
Alternately, one could swap the motors by swapping values in aa/bb. Or one
could map the motors anywhere to cc/dd/ee/ff (this will increase the command
length in digital mode, hence changing digital mode ID from 41h to 42h or 43h).
Or, one could map further rumble motors or other outputs to the six bytes (if
any such controller would exist).
In the initial state, aa..ff are all FFh, and the controller does then use the
old rumble control method (with only one motor). However, that old method gets
disabled once when having messed with config commands (unknown if/how one can
re-enable the old method by software).

Unknown Dualshock2 Vibration
Dualshock2 does reportedly have "two more levels of vibration", unknown what
that means and if it's used by any PSX or PS2 games... it might refer to the
small motor which usually has only 2 levels (on/off) and might have 4 levels
(fast/med/slow/off) on dualshock2... but, if so, it's unknown how to
control/unlock that feature.
Also, the PSone controller (SCPH-110) appear to have been released shortly
after Dualshock2, unknown if that means that it might have that feature, too.

Power Consumption
The power consumtion should not exceed "60 units" (when connecting more than 2
joypads via Multitaps, one must take care not to enable too many motors
simultaneously).
Config commands can be used to obtain the number of motors (Command 45h), and
the power consumption per motor (Command 46h aka PadInfoAct).

Note
Rumble is a potentially annoying feature, so games that do support rumble
should also include an option to disable it.

Controllers - Analog Buttons (Dualshock2)
-----------------------------------------

Dualshock2 has three new commands (40h,41h,4Fh) for configuring analog buttons.
Additionally, Command 45h does return a different type byte for Dualshock2.
Dualshock2 is a PS2 controller. However, it can be also used with PSX games
(either by connecting the controller to a PSX console, or by playing a PSX game
on a PS2 console).
The analog button feature is reportedly rarely used by PS2 games (and there
aren't any PSX games known to use it).

Config Mode - Command 40h "@" Dualshock2: Get/Set ButtonAttr?
  Send  01h 40h 00h Idx Val 00h 00h 00h 00h  ;<-- Set NEW Val, array[Idx]=Val
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h Val 00h 00h 00h  ;<-- Old Val (or FFh when Idx>0Bh)
Allows to change twelve 3bit values (with Idx=00h..0Bh, and Val=00h..03h).
Default is Val=02h. Purpose is unknown, the 12 values might be related to the
12 analog buttons, but there is no noticable difference between Val=0,1,2,3.
Maybe it does have some subtle effects on things like...
  Digital button sensitivity, or Analog button sensitivity, or
  Analog button bit-depth/conversion speed, or something else?

Config Mode - Command 41h "A" Dualshock2: Get Reply Capabilities
  Send  01h 41h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah FFh FFh 03h 00h 00h 00h
This seems to return a constant bitmask indicating which reply bytes can be
enabled/disabled via Command 4Fh (ie. 3FFFFh = 18 bits).

Config Mode - Command 4Fh "O" Dualshock2: Set ReplyProtocol
  Send  01h 41h 00h aa  bb  cc  dd  ee  ff
  Reply HiZ F3h 5Ah 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h
This can output some 48bit value (bit0=aa.bit0, bit47=ff.bit7), used to
enable/disable Reply bytes in the controller read command (Command 42h).
  -      HighZ                   (always transferred)      1st byte
  -      ID/Mode/Len             (always transferred)      2nd byte
  -      5Ah                     (always transferred)      3rd byte
  0      LSB of digital buttons  (0=No, 1=Yes)             4th byte
  1      MSB of digital buttons  (0=No, 1=Yes)             5th byte
  2      RightJoyX               (0=No, 1=Yes)             6th byte
  3      RightJoyY               (0=No, 1=Yes)             7th byte
  4      LeftJoyX                (0=No, 1=Yes)             8th byte
  5      LeftJoyY                (0=No, 1=Yes)             9th byte
  6      DPAD Right              (0=No, 1=Yes) button 00h  10th byte
  7      DPAD Left               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 01h  11th byte
  8      DPAD Uup                (0=No, 1=Yes) button 02h  12th byte
  9      DPAD Down               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 03h  13th byte
  10     Button /\               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 04h  14th byte
  11     Button ()               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 05h  15th byte
  12     Button ><               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 06h  16th byte
  13     Button []               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 07h  17th byte
  14     Button L1               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 08h  18th byte
  15     Button R1               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 09h  19th byte
  16     Button L2               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 0Ah  20th byte
  17     Button R2               (0=No, 1=Yes) button 0Bh  21st byte
  18-39  Must be 0 (otherwise command is ignored)
  40-47  Unknown (no effect?)
Usually, one would use one of the following command/values:
  Send  01h 41h 00h 03h 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h  Digital buttons
  Send  01h 41h 00h 3Fh 00h 00h 00h 00h 00h  Digital buttons + analog sticks
  Send  01h 41h 00h FFh FFh 03h 00h 00h 00h  Enable all 18 input bytes
The transfer order is 1st..21st byte as shown above (unless some bits are
cleared, eg. if bit0-5=0 and bit6=1 then DPAD Right would appear as 4th byte
instead of 10th byte). The command length increases/decreases depending on the
number of enabled bits. The transfer length is always 3+N*2 bytes (including a
00h padding byte when the number of enabled bits is odd). The analog mode ID
byte changes depending on number of halfwords.
CAUTION: Sending Command 44h does RESET the Command 4Fh setting (either to
DigitalMode=000003h or AnalogMode=00003Fh; same happens when toggling mode via
Analog button).

Note: Some Dualshock2 Config Mode commands do occassionally send 00h, 5Ah, or
FFh as last (9th) reply byte (unknown if that is some error/status thing, or
garbage).

Analog Button Sensitivity
The pressure sensors are rather imprecise and results may vary on various
factors, including the pressure angle.
  00h       Button released
  01h..2Fh  Normal (soft) pressure
  30h..FEh  Medium pressure
  FFh       Hard pressure
Software can safely distinguish between soft and hard pressure.
Medium pressure is less predictably: The values do not increase linearily, it's
difficult to apply a specific amount of medium pressure (such like 80h..9Fh),
increasing pressure may sometimes jump from 24h to FFh, completely skipping the
medium range.
Relying on the medium range might work for accelleration buttons (where the
user could still adjust the pressure when the accelleration is too high or too
low); but it would be very bad practice to assign irreversible actions to
medium pressure (such like Soft=Load, Medium=Save, Hard=Quit).

Digital Button Sensitivity
Digital inputs are converting the analog inputs as so:
  Analog=00h      --> not pressed
  Analog=01h..FFh --> pressed (no matter if soft, medium, or hard pressure)
Digital inputs are working even when also having analog input enabled for the
same button.

See also
  https://gist.github.com/scanlime/5042071 - tech (=mentions unknown details)
  https://store.curiousinventor.com/guides/PS2/ - guide (=omits unknown stuff)

Controllers - Dance Mats
------------------------

PSX Dance Mats are essentially normal joypads with uncommonly arranged buttons,
the huge mats are meant to be put on the floor, so the user could step on them.

Dance Mat vs Joypad Compatibility
There are some differences to normal joypads: First of, the L1/L2/R1/R2
shoulder buttons are missing in most variants. And, the mats are allowing to
push Left+Right and Up+Down at once, combinations that aren't mechanically
possible on normal joypads (some dancing games do actually require those
combinations, whilst some joypad games may get confused on them).

Dance Mat Unknown Things
Unknown if the mat was sold in japan, and if so, with which SLPH/SCPH number.
Unknown if the mat's middle field is also having a button assigned.
Unknown if the mat is having a special controller ID, or if there are other
ways to detect mats (the mats are said to be compatible with skateboard games,
so the mats are probably identifying themselves as normal digital joypad;
assuming that those skateboard games haven't been specifically designed for
mats).

Dance Mat Games
  D.D.R. Dance Dance Revolution 2nd Remix
  (and maybe whatever further games)
The mats can be reportedly also used with whatever skateboard games.

Dance Mat Variants
There is the US version (DDR Dance Pad, SLUH-00071), and a slightly different
European version (Official Dance Mat, SLEH-00023: shiny latex style with
perverted colors, and Start/Select arranged differently). The japanese version
(RU017) resembles the US version, but without Triangle/Square symbols drawn in
lower left/right edges.
And there is a handheld version (with additional L1/L2/R2/R1 buttons; maybe
unlicensed; produced as MINI DDR, and also as Venom Mini Dance Pad).

Stay Cool?
Despite of the "Stay Cool!" slogan, the mat wasn't very cool - not at all! It
offered only two steps back-and-forth, and also allowed to do extremly uncool
side-steps. Not to mention that it would melt when dropping a burning cigarette
on it. Stay Away!

Controllers - Fishing Controllers
---------------------------------

The fishing rods are (next to lightguns) some of the more openly martial
playstation controllers - using the credo that "as long as you aren't using
dynamite: it's okay to kill them cause they don't have any feelings."

Logos on CD Covers
US Fishing games should have a "SLUH-00063" logo. European Fishing games don't
have any fishing logos; apparently fishing controllers haven't been officially
released/supported in Europe.
Japanese Fishing games can have a bunch of logos: Usually BANC-0001 or
SLPH-00100 (or both).
Moreover, some japanese games have a yellow/green fishing logo with japanese
text (found on Perfect Fishing: Bass Fishing, Perfect Fishing: Rock Fishing,
Simple 1500 Series Vol. 29: The Tsuri, Super Bass Fishing) (unknown if that
logo refer to other special hardware, or if it means the "normal" BANC-0001 or
SLPH-00100 controllers.
And Moreover, some japanese games have some sort of "headset" logos with
japanese text, these seem to have same meaning as SLPH-00100; as indicated by
photos on CD cover of Tsuwadou Keiryuu Mizuumihen (Best Edition) (2000); that
CD cover also has a "headset 2" logo, which seems to mean a newer PS2 variant
of the SLPH-00100.

PSX Fishing Controllers
  ASCII ASC-0514TR aka ASCII SLPH-00100 (silver)
  ASCII ASC-0521TR2 (silver) (similar to SLPH-00100, with additional hardware)
  agetec SLUS-00063 (silver) (US version of ASCII's SLPH-00100 controller)
  Bandai BANC-0001 (dark gray/blue) (has less buttons than ASCII/agetec)
  Interact Fission (light gray/blue)(similar to ASCII/agetec, 2 extra buttons?)
  Naki (transparent blue) (looks like a clone of the ASCII/agetec controllers)
  SAMMY SMY-0506FS (looks same as ASC-0521TR2)
  SAMMY SMY-0511FS (shortened joystick, rearranged /\,[],(),>< buttons)
  Hori HPS-97/HPS-98 (black/gray) (a fishing rod attached to a plastic fish)
Of these, the ASCII/agetec controllers seem to be most popular (and most
commonly supported). The Bandai contoller is also supported by a couple of
games (though the Bandai controller itself seems to be quite rare). The
Interact/Naki controllers are probably just clones of the ASCII/agetec ones.
The Hori controller is quite rare (and with its string and plastic fish, it's
apparently working completely different than the other fishing controllers).

Tech Info (all unknown)
Unknown how to detect fishing controllers.
Unknown how to read buttons, joystick, crank, motion sensors.
Unknown how to control rumble/vibration.
Unknown if/how Bandai differs from ASCII/agetec (aside from less buttons).
Unknown how the Hori thing works.

Controllers - Fishing Controllers - ASC-0521TR2
-----------------------------------------------

Controller Modes
  Digital Joypad mode (power-up default)
  Mode0 (".")
  Mode1 ("1")
  Mode2 ("2")

Fishing Digital Mode
  __Halfword 0 (Controller Info)_______________________________________________
  0-15  Controller Info  (5A41h=digital)
  __Halfword 1 (Digital Switches)______________________________________________
  0-15  Buttons (with Joystick mapped as DPAD) (and L3 mapped to () button)
Missing: Reel Wheel, Star wheel, 3-axis Piezo sensor, Pendulums
Restrictions: Analog stick and L3 works as DPAD and () button only

Fishing Mode 0
  __Halfword 0 (Controller Info)_______________________________________________
  0-15  Controller Info  (5A73h=analog/pad)
  __Halfword 1 (Digital Switches)______________________________________________
  0-15  Buttons (with Joystick mapped as DPAD) (and L3 mapped to () button)
  __Halfword 2 (Right joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)_________
  0-7   adc0 Fixed      (always 80h=Center)
  8-15  adc1 Reel Wheel (00h=Backward, 80h=Stopped, FFh=Forward)
  __Halfword 3 (Left joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)__________
  0-7   adc2 Pendulum X (00h=Left, 80h=Center, FFh=Right)
  8-15  adc3 Pendulum Y (00h=Down, 80h=Center, FFh=Up)
Motor Control bytes:
  Byte00.bit0    Small vibration motor (0=Off, 1=On)
  Byte01.bit7-0  Big vibration motor   (0=Off, FFh=Max)
Missing: Star wheel, 3-axis Piezo sensor, Band brake
Restrictions: Analog stick and L3 works as DPAD and () button only

Fishing Mode 1
  __Halfword 0 (Controller Info)_______________________________________________
  0-15  Controller Info  (5AE5h=custom/fishing)
  __Halfword 1 (Digital Switches)______________________________________________
  0-15  Buttons (with DPAD bits always released) (and L3 mapped as such)
  __Halfword 2 (Right joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)_________
  0-7   adc0 Fixed      (always 80h=Center)
  8-15  adc1 Fixed      (always 80h=Center)
  __Halfword 3 (Left joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)__________
  0-7   adc2 Joystick X (00h=Left, 80h=Center, FFh=Right)
  8-15  adc3 Joystick Y (00h=Up,   80h=Center, FFh=Down)
  __Halfword 4
  0-7   adc4 3-Axis sensor (00h, 80h=Center, FFh)
  8-15  adc5 3-Axis sensor (00h, 80h=Center, FFh)
  __Halfword 5
  0-7   adc6 3-Axis sensor (00h, 80h=Center, FFh)
  8-15  adc7 Reel Wheel (00h=Stopped, FFh=Forward)
Motor Control bytes:
  Byte00.bit0    Small vibration motor (0=Off, 1=On)
  Byte01.bit7-0  Big vibration motor   (0=Off, FFh=Max)
Missing: Star wheel, Pendulums, Band brake
Restrictions: Reel Wheel supports forward only (backward is ignored)

Fishing Mode 2
  __Halfword 0 (Controller Info)_______________________________________________
  0-15  Controller Info  (5A73h=analog/pad) (with DPAD LT/RT used as extra ID)
  __Halfword 1 (Digital Switches)______________________________________________
  0-15  Buttons (UP/DN=Star wheel, LT/RT=Stuck, and L3 mapped as such)
  __Halfword 2 (Right joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)_________
  0-2   adc  Joystick Y (upper 3bit) (00h=Up,   04h=Center, 07h=Down)
  3-7   adc  Joystick X (5bit)       (00h=Left, 10h=Center, 1Fh=Right)
  8     adc  Pendulum Y (upper 1bit) (00h=Down, 10h=Center, 1Fh=Up)
  9-13  adc  Pendulum X (5bit)       (00h=Left, 10h=Center, 1Fh=Right)
  14-15 adc  Joystick Y (lower 2bit) (to be merged with upper 3bit)
  __Halfword 3 (Left joystick) (analog pad/stick in analog mode only)__________
  0-3   adc  3-Axis sensor Y  (4bit) (00h, 08h=Center, 0Fh)
  4-7   adc  Pendulum Y (lower 4bit) (to be merged with upper 1bit)
  8-11  adc  Reel Wheel     (..bit?) (00h=Stopped, 0xh=Forward)
  12-15 adc  3-Axis sensor X  (4bit) (00h, 08h=Center, 0Fh)
Motor Control bytes:
  Byte00.bit0    Small vibration motor (0=Off, 1=On)
  Byte01.bit7-4  Big vibration motor   (0=Off, 0Fh=Max)
  Byte01.bit3-0  Band brake motor      (0=Off, 0Fh=Max)
Missing: 3rd axis of 3-axis Piezo sensor
Restrictions: Reel Wheel supports forward only (backward is ignored)
Accuracy: The inputs/outputs are only 4bit or 5bit wide (instead of 8bit)
Issues: Sometimes returns garbage... Timings problems?

Switch Changes
Changing the switch position appears to be intended to reset the controller
into digital mode, however, there are several flaws:
  Mode 0: Works
  Mode 1: Stays in analog mode (if analog mode was enabled)
  Mode 2: Works, but DPAD stays stuck at UP/DN=Released, LT/RT=Pressed)
Alongsides, changing the mode switch changes the 5Ah byte to 00h to indicate
mode changes (similar as when pressing Analog button on analog pads).

Controllers - Mahjong and Card Game Controllers
-----------------------------------------------

The Mahjong & Card Game controllers contain small LCD displays for showing the
player's cards/tiles (without other players seeing them when playing in 2-4
player mode). Obviously, it's a waste of everything, and it would be easier and
cheaper to use a real card game.

Hori Wai Wai Jansou Controller (for Mahjong games)
This controller is supported by two games (Wai Wai Jansou, Wai Wai 3-nin Uchi
Mahjong). There are at least four contoller versions: The Set includes
clear/red & clear/green. Additionally, clear/gray & clear/blue are sold
separately. The different colors do apply to the bottom-side of the case, which
is barely visible when looking at the transparent top-side.
  HPS-90  Wai Wai Jansou CDROM
  HPS-91  Wai Wai Jansou Set (CDROM with two Jansou controllers)
  HPS-92  Wai Wai Jansou Controller (clear/gray)
  HPS-93  Wai Wai Jansou Controller (clear/blue)
  HPS-94  Wai Wai Jansou Controller (..unknown color..)
  HPS-95  Wai Wai Jansou Controller (..unknown color..)
  HPS-116 Wai Wai 3-nin Uchi Mahjong Set (CDROM with two Jansou Controllers)
   ______________________________________
  |                                      |
  |   .-----------------------------.    |
  |   |   #######################   |    |  LCD display
  |   |__________.---------.________|    |  with DPAD and nine buttons
  |     _                                |
  |   _| |_       SEL START          O   |
  |  |_   _| _                 _   O   O |
  |    |_|  (_)               (_)    O   |
  |__________B_________________A___O_____|
Unknown if somebody can translate the markings on the five yellow buttons
Unknown if the controller supports config commands
Unknown how to detect the controller

Some info: http://www.psxdev.net/forum/viewtopic.php?t=3432

This controller is supported by only one game (Wai Wai Trump Taisen), and there
seems to be only one controller version.
  HPS-104 Wai Wai Trump Taisen CDROM
  HPS-105 Wai Wai Trump Taisen Set (CDROM with two Trump Controllers)

Unknown if/how the protocol differs from Wai Wai Jansou

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor (Mobile Internet)
----------------------------------------------

The I-Mode Adaptor cable (SCPH-10180) allows to connect an I-mode compatible
mobile phone to the playstation's controller port; granting a mobile internet
connection to japanese games.

--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Controller Port Commands
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Connect Messages
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Transfer Messages
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - TLP Transport Layer
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - HTTP Requests/Replies
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Software
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Misc
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Libimode Library
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Unknown Features
--> Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - References

Pinouts
--> Pinouts - Component List and Chipset Pin-Outs for I-Mode Cable SCPH-10180

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Controller Port Commands
-------------------------------------------------------

Controller Port Commands
There are two data streams:
  Small Control Messages     (sent/received via command 14h, 15h, or 18h)
  Large 80h-byte Data Blocks (sent/received via command 14h)
The games are sending data at 500kbit/s (except, the first byte (41h) should be
always sent at 250kbit/s, to properly deselect controllers or memory cards).
Regardless, the transfer is ways slower: The 88h-byte messages contain only
58h-byte actual data (500*58h/88h = 323kbit/s), and the existing PSX software
transfers only one such packet per vblank (58h*8*60 = 42kbit/s), and I-Mode is
reportedly supporting only 9.6kbit/s for TLP messages).
BUG: The 1st reply byte is 00h (rather than HighZ), that reply byte will occur
even when trying to access other hardware like joypads or memory cards.

Command 11h (len=5) - Unknown (unused in Hamster Club-i)
  Send  41h 11h (0) (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah 8Eh Stat[2]
Unknown. Hamster Club-i contains some (unused) code for sending this command;
without any parameters, and without checking the response (which seems to be
always 8Eh, plus Stat[2]).

Command 12h (len=7) - Config ...
  Send  41h 12h NewX NewY (0)  (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah 6Fh  NewX NewY Stat[2]
Parameters:
  X = usually/always 00h (but can be 00h..04h)               (00h..04h)
  Y = usually 03h=UsedBeforeShutdown, or 06h=UsedAfterWakeup (00h..FFh)
Reply:
  Always 6Fh, followed by echoing the (newly written) parameter values
  (whereas, X=05h..FFh gets forcefully changed to X=00h)
X=00h..04h gets translated to 09h,12h,24h,48h,91h, which is then further
multiplied/divided and somehow treated as a "length" value, which seems to
affect Command 15h and 18h.

Command 13h (len=5) - Wakeup (sets Stat[2] to 01h,00h)
  Send  41h 13h 0Fh (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah C0h Stat[2]
Parameters:
  Usually/always 0Fh     ;XXX but in browser: initially 03h, later 0Fh

Command 14h (len=88h) - Dual-Stream Transfer
  Send  41h 14h Data[80h] MsgLen Msg[19h] Chksum (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah Data[80h] MsgLen Msg[19h] Chksum Stat[2]
Parameters:
  Data[80h] = Data Stream bytes (see below)
  Msglen    = 0..2      ;Hamster Club-i uses only 0..1 for sending though
  Msg[2]    = Message bytes
  Chksum    = Above 83h bytes XORed together
The Data[80h] part can contain one or more data snippets:
  00h 1   1st Snippet Length (1..58h, plus bit7=LastSnippetFlag) ;\
  01h ..  1st Snippet Data                                       ;
  ... 1   2nd Snippet Length (1..58h, plus bit7=LastSnippetFlag) ;
  ... ..  2nd Snippet Data                                       ; if any
  ... 1   3rd Snippet Length (1..58h, plus bit7=LastSnippetFlag) ;
  ... ..  3rd Snippet Data                                       ;
  ... ..  etc.                                                   ;/
  ... 1   End marker (00h) (aka snippet length zero)             ;\end
  ... ..  Unused padding                                         ;/
  7Fh 1   Flags (bit0=PhoneBusy)                                 ;-flags
Packets bigger than 58h bytes can occupy multiple snippets (length bit7=1
indicates the final snippet).
The last 2 data bytes (of the last snippet) contain a CRC16_CCITT_REVERSE in
little-endian, with initial value FFFFh, and result XORed by FFFFh.

Command 15h (len=1Fh) - Single-Stream Transfer
  Send  41h 15h MsgLen Msg[19h] Chksum (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah MsgLen Msg[19h] Chksum Stat[2]
Parameters:
  Msglen   = 0..19h
  Msg[19h] = Message bytes
  Chksum   = Above 1Ah bytes XORed together

Command 16h (len=5) - Config Single/Dual-Stream Mode
  Send  41h 16h MODE (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah 4Ah  Stat[2]
Parameters:
  MODE = Indicates if Command 14h or 15h will be used (0=Cmd15h, 1=Cmd14h)

Command 17h (len=5) - Config Clear/Reset
  Send  41h 17h FLAG (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah 56h  Stat[2]
FLAG (03h or 0Ch or 0Fh or 10h):
  bit0  Clear Send queue   ;\clear queue inside of PSX (probably implies
  bit1  Clear Recv queue   ;/request to also clear queue in Fujitsu chip)
  bit2  Ack/swap/apply/discard TX block number?   ;\for 80h-byte data blocks
  bit3  Ack/swap/apply/discard RX block number?   ;/
  bit4  Reset/Shutdown (changes Stat[2] to 00h,00h)

Command 18h (len=6) - Single-Stream Transfer (unused in Hamster Club-i)
  Send  41h 18h MsgLen Msg[1] (0) (0)
  Reply 00h 5Ah MsgLen Msg[1] Stat[2]
Seems to be same as Command 15h, but MsgLen can be only 0..1 bytes, and without
checksum.

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Connect Messages
-----------------------------------------------

I-Mode Messages
Sending/receiving these messages can be done via command 14h, 15h, and/or 18h.
The messages start with an 8bit value (eg. 85h), followed by several "4bit
parameter bytes" (which have the upper 4bits set to zero).

Send:
  85h,01h,01h,02h,plain_random[8],00h,03h,00h,00h,01h    ;-AUTH_START_REQ
  85h,01h,04h,02h,crypted_random[8]                      ;-AUTH_CRYPT_REQ
  85h,01h,05h,02h                                        ;-AUTH_DONE
  85h,01h,06h                                            ;-DEAUTH_REQ
  8Eh     ;<-- is that same 8Eh as in Keitai Eddy?       ;-AUTH_PING_REQ
  F2h,00h,01h,02h,08h,00h,00h,00h,00h                    ;-GW_CONNECT_REQ
  F2h,00h,01h,02h,00h,00h,00h,00h,00h                    ;-GW_DISCONNECT_REQ
  F2h,00h,01h,02h,01h,00h,00h,00h,00h  ;used in browser  ;-GW_PING_REQ
  A8h     ;<-- used in the browser, after entering a 4-digit PIN number

Recv messages (based on code in Hamster Club-i):
  38h,02h                           ;return 06h    ;-Wokeup             ;\
  85h,01h,02h,x,x,H,L,dat(HL)       ;return 02h    ;-AUTH_CRYPT_ACK     ;
  85h,01h,03h,data[3]               ;return 01h    ;-AUTH_error/busy?   ;
  85h,01h,04h,x,dat(8),H,L,dat(HL)  ;return 03h    ;-AUTH_START_ACK     ; STATE
  85h,01h,07h                       ;return 04h    ;-DEAUTH_ACK         ;
  F1h,00h,03h,x,H,L,dat(HL)      ;return 05h,[0Ah] ;state [0Ah]=1=okay? ;
  F2h,00h,02h,x,08h,x,H,L,dat(HL+4) ;return 0Ah    ;-GW_CONNECT_ACK     ;
  F2h,00h,02h,x,00h,x,H,L,dat(HL+4) ;return 0Bh    ;-GW_DISCONNECT_ACK  ;
  F2h,00h,02h,x,01h,x,H,L,dat(1+HL) ;return 0Dh    ;-GW_PING_ACK        ;
  F2h,00h,02h,x,09h,x,H,L,dat(1+HL) ;return 0Dh    ;-GW_PING_ACK, too?  ;
  F2h,00h,03h,..                    ;return 0Ch  ;ready to GW_CONNECT ? ;/
  21h,...     ;used by browser      ;return 14h, modus=0                ;\
  80h         ;not implemented      ;return 1Fh, modus=0                ;
  81h                               ;return 20h, modus=0                ;
  8Ah,..      ;not implemented      ;return 21h, modus=0                ;
  8Bh,..                            ;return 22h, modus=0                ; ?
  A4h,..                            ;return 18h, modus=0                ;
  A5h,..                            ;return 0, modus=40h                ;
  A6h                               ;return 17h, modus=0                ;
  A7h                               ;return 16h, modus=0                ;
  AAh,..      ;\multiple uses       ;return 15h                         ;
  AAh,..      ; depending on        ;return 0, modus=0                  ;
  AAh         ;/state/flags         ;return 23h, modus=0 ;AUTH_PING_ACK ;
  E0h,..      ;\terminated          ;return 0, set modus and 40h or 1   ;
  E6h,..      ;/by AAh ?            ;return 0, set modus and 50h or 2   ;/
  C0h..CFh                          ;ignored                            ;\
  D1h,...                           ;whatever                           ; data?
  00h..0Fh                          ;data bytes?                        ;/

Recv message format (based on message-length tables in Hamster Club-i):
  C0h..CFh

  35h,x, ... , endflag(bit0)

  6Ch,08h
  6Ch,0Ah,data[5+1+3],H,L,data[HL*2],H,L,[HL*2]  ;?
  6Ch,0Ch
  6Ch,0Dh,data[24h]
  6Ch,0Eh, ... , endflag(bit0)
  6Eh,data[1]
  80h
  81h

  85h,x,02h,x,x,H,L,data[HL]
  85h,x,03h,data[3]
  85h,x,04h,00h,data[9],H,L,data[HL]

  missing A5h
  A6h

  missing AAh (but may work as breakout code and ping_ack?)
  missing D1h (but may work as breakout code?)

  E2h,x, ... ,AAh    ;with end_code=AAh
  missing E6h        ;with end_code=AAh
  E7h,data[2]

  F1h,x,03h,x,H,L,data[HL]
  F1h,x,04h,data[2]

  F2h,x,02h,x,09h,x,H,L,data[HL+1]
  F2h,x,03h,x,x,H,L,data[HL]
Whereas,
  x   = don't care for length (but actual code may insist on specific values)
  H,L = high/low nibbles of HL length value
  missing = not handled in length table (but exists in code)
The length table contains many messages that aren't handled in actual code.

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Transfer Messages
------------------------------------------------

I-Mode Messages on 80h-byte stream
Sending/receiving these messages can be done via 58h-byte snippet(s) in the
80h-byte portion of Command 14h.
Commands/Replies are decoded by examining the first 2-3 bytes of the message.
The first byte must be 01h or 03h (01 or 11 binary). The second byte consists
of several bitfields (with the overall response type in lower 1-2 bits). The
TLP messages include a third byte (hardcoded to 01h in the connect code).

I-Mode Send Messages on 80h-byte stream
  01h,BBB*20h+nnn*2,01h,<TLP_MESSAGE>,crc16            req=00xh ;-TLP messages
  01h,BBB*20h+01h,crc16 --> error ?                             ;\
  0xh,BBB*20h+x5h,crc16 --> error ?                    req=020h ;
  01h,BBB*20h+09h,crc16 --> error_wrong_blkno_lsb      req=040h ; handshake
  01h,BBB*20h+11h,crc16 --> error_no_reply                      ; errors
  03h,BBB*20h+01h,crc16 --> transfer_timer             req=010h ;
  03h,BBB*20h+xxh,crc16 --> error ?                             ;/
  0xh,1Fh,crc16         --> unknown                    req=400h ;\
  01h,3Fh,crc16         --> GW_CONNECT_REQ             req=080h ;
  01h,53h,crc16         --> GW_DISCONNECT_REQ          req=100h ; control
  0xh,73h,crc16         --> unknown                    req=200h ;
  03h,87h,0xh,e,a,crc16 --> blkno (expected,actual)    req=800h ;/

I-Mode Reply Messages on 80h-byte stream
Below are the supported replies (in binary):
  x1_bbb0nnn0_00000001    event=0Fh (matching blkno)            ;\
  x1_bbb0xxx0             event=10h (wrong blkno in bit1-3)     ; TLP
  x1_bbb1nnn0_00000001    event=11h (matching blkno)            ; messages
  x1_bbb1xxx0             event=12h (wrong blkno in bit1-3)     ;/
  x1_bbb00001 (aka 01h)   event=14h                             ;\
  x1_bbb00101 (aka 05h)   event=17h                             ;
  x1_bbb01001 (aka 09h)   event=1Ah                             ; handshake
  01_bbb10001 (aka 11h)   event=13h                             ; errors?
  11_bbb10001 (aka 11h)   event=15h                             ;
  01_bbb10101 (aka 15h)   event=16h                             ;
  11_bbb10101 (aka 15h)   event=18h                             ;
  01_bbb11001 (aka 19h)   event=19h (error_wrong_blkno_lsb_ack?);
  11_bbb11001 (aka 19h)   event=1Bh                             ;
  x1_bbb0xx01 (other)     event=27h (invalid)                   ;
  01_bbb1xx01 (other)     event=26h (invalid)                   ;
  11_bbb1xx01 (other)     event=28h (invalid)                   ;/
  01_00001111 (aka_0Fh)   event=23h (force disconnect?)         ;\
  11_00001111 (aka 0Fh)   event=27h (invalid)                   ;
  01_00011111 (aka 1Fh)   event=22h (GW_DISCONNECT_ACK)         ;
  11_00011111 (aka 1Fh)   event=26h (invalid)                   ; control
  x1_00101111 (aka 2Fh)   event=1Eh                             ;
  01_00111111 (aka 3Fh)   event=26h (invalid)                   ;
  11_00111111 (aka 3Fh)   event=1Fh                             ;
  x1_01000011 (aka 43h)   event=20h                             ;
  11_01010011 (aka 53h)   event=21h                             ;
  01_01010011 (aka 53h)   event=26h (invalid)                   ;
  x1_01100011 (aka 63h)   event=1Dh                             ;
  01_01110011 (aka 73h)   event=1Ch (GW_CONNECT_ACK)            ;
  11_01110011 (aka 73h)   event=None/07h/08h (error, ignore/retry/giveup)
  01_10000111 (aka 87h)   event=25h (force disconnect?)         ;
  11_10000111 (aka 87h)   event=27h (invalid)                   ;
  01_10010111 (aka 97h)   event=24h (force disconnect?)         ;
  11_10010111 (aka 97h)   event=26h (invalid)                   ;
  x1_xxx0xx11 (other)     event=27h (invalid)                   ;
  01_xxx1xx11 (other)     event=26h (invalid)                   ;
  11_xxx1xx11 (other)     event=28h (invalid)                   ;/
  xxxxxxxx (other)        ignored (1st byte other than 01h or 03h or 10h+x)
  xxx1xxx0                ignored single-byte reply, do NOT reload timeouts
  xxxxxxxx (other)        ignored single-byte reply, but DO reload timeouts
  xxxxxxxx_xxxxxxxx       reload timeouts (on any reply with 2 or more bytes)
The replies are triggering the events that are shown above, which are then
triggering a send_request (numbered 10h, 20h, 40h, 80h, 100h, 200h, 400h,
800h). That send_request does then trigger event 0Ah..0Eh. And those events are
then using the send_request or other flags to decide which command message they
want to send. Those commands are usually 2 or 5 bytes tall (event 0Ah,0Bh are
additionally sending larger commands/packets)

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - TLP Transport Layer
--------------------------------------------------

I-Mode Packets
TLP packets are send via one of the Command 14h commands:
  000h 3    Send Command (01h,BBB*20h+NNN*2,01h) (imode/cable-specific command)
  003h ..   TLP Packet (contains Checksum, Message Type, ..., Data)
  ...  2    CRC16_CCITT_REVERSE ;little endian, initial=FFFFh, result XOR FFFFh
The second byte consists of:
  bit0    must be 0 (indicates TLP_messages)
  bit1-3  outgoing block number (increased after each message, 0 at gw_connect)
  bit4    unknown (usually 0)
  bit5-7  remote block number (from bit1-3 of remote message) (..plus 0..1 ?)

Logic State
The Logic State byte indicates presence of optional components that will be
appended to the message (although most Message Types are using fixed values for
the Logic State bits).
  bit4-7 unused (usually zero)
  bit3   allowed in Type=10h
  bit2   unknown, must be set for Type=11h
  bit1   allowed in Type=11h,20h,21h,30h (and implied for Type=31h)
  bit0   allowed in Type=10h,11h,20h,30h
Transmit Segment has flags in upper 2bit, which should be usually both set for
the normal communication mode (in other modes the bits seem to be used to
indicate first and last segment).

Message Type 10h - TLP_CONNECT_REQ (0Eh+N bytes, Send-only)
This does invoke a HTTP connection, the Transmit Data contains the HTTP request
header (eg. GET/POST command, which should hopefully fit into 1400 bytes), plus
first some bytes of HTTP request body (if any).
  000h 2    Checksum (sum of following 16bit values plus carry-outs, XOR FFFFh)
  002h 1    Message Type        (10h)
  003h 1    Service Identifier  (0Ah) (whatever, maybe means 0Ah=HTTP)
  004h 1    Logical Number      (01h) (bit0-6=Connection, bit7=Flag?)
  005h 1    Communication Mode  (01h) (bit0-1=Mode, bit2-7=Value?)
  006h 1    Communication Parameters[0] (01h)
  007h 1    Communication Parameters[1] (01h)
  008h 1    Communication Parameters[2] (8Ch) max packet size/10, 8Ch=1400 byte
  009h 1    Communication Parameters[3] (01h)
  00Ah 1    Communication Parameters[4] (FFh) timeout/1000 or so?
  00Bh 1    Communication Parameters[5] (00h)
  00Ch 1    Communication Parameters[6] (0Ah)
  00Dh 1    Logic State (09h) (indicates presence of below optional components)
  ...  2    Operator Specific Information  (4821h)     ;-when bit3=1 ;\
  ...  (1)  Requested Segment Number       (-)         ;-when bit1=1 ;
  ...  1    Transmit Segment Number+Flags  (C0h)       ;\            ; Optional
  ...  2    Transmit Length (1..1400)      (03B7h)     ; when bit0=1 ;
  ...  LEN  Transmit Data ("POST http://ne-net.com/"..);/            ;/
The lower 7bit of the Logical Number contain a Connection ID in range 01h..7Fh
(this value is incremented for each new connection; unknown if one could use
multiple connections; the PSX games/browser do always DISCONNECT before doing a
new CONNECT).

Message Type 11h - TLP_CONNECT_ACK (0Dh+N bytes, Recv-only)
This does acknowledge a HTTP connection, the Transmit Data contains the HTTP
response header (usually with HTTP/1.0 200 OK, and Content-Length, and other
info), plus first some bytes of HTTP response body (if any).
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (11h)
  003h 1    Logical Number      (01h)
  004h 1    Communication Mode  (01h)     ;\
  005h 1    Communication Parameters[0]   ;
  006h 1    Communication Parameters[1]   ; these can/may/should use same
  007h 1    Communication Parameters[2]   ; values as in message type 10h
  008h 1    Communication Parameters[3]   ;
  009h 1    Communication Parameters[4]   ;
  00Ah 1    Communication Parameters[5]   ;
  00Bh 1    Communication Parameters[6]   ;/
  00Ch 1    Logic State (07h) (indicates presence of below optional components)
  ...  (2)  Operator Specific Information (-)          ;-when bit3=1 ;\
  ...  1    Requested Segment Number (0..3Fh)          ;-when bit1=1 ;
  ...  1    Transmit Segment Number  (0..3Fh+Flags)    ;\            ; Optional
  ...  2    Transmit Length (big-endian)               ; when bit0=1 ;
  ...  ..   Transmit Data ("HTTP/1.0 200 OK"..)        ;/            ;/

Message Type 12h - TLP_CONNECT_REJECT (05h bytes, Recv-only)
This is supposedly used for rejecting connections (possible reasons might be
invalid domain name, or perhaps exceeding monthly traffic limit).
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (12h)
  003h 1    Logical Number
  004h 1    Disconnect Reason (00h..08h)

Message Type 20h - TLP_DISCONNECT_REQ (06h+N bytes, Recv/Send)
Message Type 21h - TLP_DISCONNECT_ACK (06h+N bytes, Recv/Send)
Disconnection can be invoked by sender or receiver (or both).
Normally, if one unit does run out of data then it will send DATA_EOF, if the
other unit does also run out of data then it will send DISCONNECT_REQ (this
behaviour is required for Hamster Club-i).
Additionally, the PSX can examine the Content-Length in HTTP response, and
throw DISCONNECT_REQ when reaching that length (this happens in NetFront
browser, and it can result in both sides sending DISCONNECT_REQ).
Additionally, the PSX can clip the Content-Length to some maximum value
(usually 10240 bytes), and throw DISCONNECT_REQ when reaching that limit.
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (20h/21h)
  003h 1    Logical Number
  004h 1    Disconnect Reason   (00h..08h) (0=Okay/Transfer completed)
  005h 1    Logic State         (usually 00h)
  ...  (2)  Operator Specific Information            ;-when bit3=1 ;\
  ...  1    Requested Segment Number (0..3Fh)        ;-when bit1=1 ; Optional
  ...  1    Transmit Segment Number  (0..3Fh+Flags)  ;\            ; usually
  ...  2    Transmit Length                          ; when bit0=1 ; none such
  ...  ..   Transmit Data                            ;/            ;/
20h/21h have same format... but 21h has extra restrictions on Logic Srate.

Message Type 30h - TLP_DATA (09h+N bytes, Recv/Send)
Used to send/receive additional HTTP data packets (additionally to the first
packet in the CONNECT messages), with increasing segment numbers.
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (30h)
  003h 1    Logical Number
  004h 1    Logic State         (usually 03h) (must be xxxx0x11 binary)
  005h 1    Requested Segment Number (0..3Fh)       ;\
  006h 1    Transmit Segment Number  (0..3Fh+Flags) ; always present because
  007h 2    Transmit Length                         ; above bit1,0 are both set
  009h ..   Transmit Data                           ;/

Message Type 31h - TLP_DATA_EOF (05h bytes, Recv/Send)
Indicates that there are no more transmit segments (and requests next segment
from opponent).
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (31h)
  003h 1    Logical Number
  004h 1    Requested Segment Number (0..3Fh) (alike as if Logic State bit1=1)

Message Type 40h - TLP_INFO (07h+N bytes, Recv-only)
Contains "info", purpose is unknown (maybe notifications about incoming voice
calls, battery state, or such things).
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (40h)
  003h 1    Service Identifier  (must be 09h, unlike as in Message Type 10h)
  004h 1    Communication Mode/Logical Number (bit0-1=Mode, bit2-7=Connection)
  005h 2    Data Length
  007h ..   Data (whatever info)

Message Type 41h - TLP_INFO_ACK (04h bytes, Send-only)
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (41h)
  003h 1    Communication Mode/Logical Number (bit0-1=Mode, bit2-7=Connection)

Message Type 50h - Unknown/Unused (06h+N bytes, Recv/Send)
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (50h)
  003h 1    Logical Number
  004h 1    Transmit Segment Number
  005h 1    Transmit SmallData Length (max 5 bytes or so?)
  006h ..   Transmit SmallData[..]    ;flagbits! (per Communication Mode 6bit)

Message Type 60h - Unknown/Unused (04h bytes, Recv/Send)
  000h 2    Checksum
  002h 1    Message Type        (60h)
  003h 1    Logical Number

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - HTTP Requests/Replies
----------------------------------------------------

HTTP versions
There are several notable HTTP versions:
  HTTP/1.0 ascii headers                        (1991)
  HTTP/1.1 ascii headers, with Host: domain     (1997)
  HTTP/2   binary headers for faster transfers  (2015)
Although released in 2001, the PSX software does still use the old HTTP/1.0
format (unknown if the I-Mode server would also accept HTTP/1.1 messages).

HTTP domains
HTTP/1.0 didn't use domain names (it did solely rely on the IP address in the
TCP/IP packets, which can be a problem when using shared IPs for virtual
domains).
HTTP/1.1 did invent a "Host: domain" entry in the HTTP header (this allows to
redirect the TCP/IP packets to the desired virtual domain) (although that
wasn't originally supported in HTTP/1.0, it's common practice to include that
"Host:" entry also in HTTP/1.0 messages).

HTTP custom I-Mode headers
I-Mode is using a simplified TLP protocol (without IP addresses, unlike
TCP/IP). This relies on including the domain name in the HTTP header (and the
I-Mode server would then care about resolving the IP address). This is using
non-standard HTTP requests as so:
  GET http://www.mydomain.net/index.html HTTP/1.0
When communicating with the outside world, the I-Mode server should parse that
request to something like this:
  GET /index.html HTTP/1.0
  Host: www.mydomain.net
Alongsides, one may also parse HTTP/1.0 to HTTP/1.1 (in case some servers
dislike old HTTP/1.0 packets, or dislike the Host: entry being used as
inofficial HTTP/1.0 extension).
And, for old PSX games, most or all old game servers do no longer exist, so one
may also need to parse the domain/path to elsewhere.

HTTP requests
The PSX programs are using either GET or POST commands. According to Sony, one
could also use HEAD. Theoretically one could also use any other HTTP commands
like PUT or DELETE (unless the I-Mode server should somehow refuse to forward
them to the actual domain).
  GET   request downloading a HTM file, or GIF file, or anything else
  POST  same as GET, with additional parameters (in request.body)
  HEAD  same as GET, but returns only response.header (without response.body)
An example HTTP request (from Hamster Club-i) looks as so:
  POST http://ne-net.com/hc/i/ps/ArenaParty.cgi HTTP/1.0  ;-request
  User-Agent: DoCoMo/1.0/ex_ps1302
  Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded         ;\for POST body
  Content-Length: 789                                     ;/
                             <blank line>                 ;-end of header
  uid=NULLGWDOCOMO&val=%0A%0A%...%CD%13%03%07             ;-POST body
Unknown if the uid "&val=..." does contain a user ID (that might have been
somehow obtained during auth/connect, or stored on the PSX memory card), or
maybe the phone or server is supposed to replace the uid "NULLGWDOCOMO" string
by the actual phone number or some other kind of docomo user id.

HTTP replies
HTTP replies contain a status code, several optional header fields like
Content-Length: and Date: terminated by a blank line, followed by the file
body. For example,
  HTTP/1.0 200 OK                                         ;-status code
  Content-Length: 123                                     ;\for body
  Content-Type: text/html                                 ;/
                             <blank line>                 ;-end of header
  <HTML><HEAD><TITLE>Hello</TITLE></HEAD>...</HTML>       ;-file body
Some servers (including problemkaputt.de) will send a HTTP/1.1 reply even when
receiving HTTP/1.0 requests (the existing PSX software seems to accept that,
without needing to parse the reply to HTTP/1.0).

HTML format
I-Mode phones are using a custom iHTML variant, which is based on cHTML (aka
compact html). This is reportedly having restrictions like not supporting
things like <TABLE>, and it's generally intended to work on old phones with
tiny LCD displays (reportedly 96x95 pixels on DoCoMo P502i) and little RAM.
When using the I-Mode phone as a "modem" for PCs or PSX consoles, browsers
could theoretically implement fully-fledged HTML support (although the PSX is
having it's own restrictions like 2Mbyte RAM and blurry TV Sets).

HTML browser
The PSX CompactNetFront browser is using 320x224 pixel resolution (actually
296x176, plus gray borders; which should work on blurry and mis-centered TV
sets; unknown if the japanese options allow to change the screen resolution for
higher resolution displays).
  The PSX browser does support HTM, TXT, GIF
  The PSX browser does support <TABLE>
  The PSX browser does not support JPG (and certainly no STJ or PNG)
  The PSX browser seems to ignore things like <B>, <HR>, <FONT SIZE>
  TXT/HTM/GIF loading aborts after 10K (10240 bytes) in http response.body

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Software
---------------------------------------

PSX I-Mode Emulation
No$psx v2.3 supports redirecting I-Mode HTTP messages to real internet (that is
HTTP only, HTTPS isn't supported, and gets redirected to HTTP where possible).
The original game servers and browser start page are no longer working, but
they can be redirected to new servers in NO$PSX.INI. For example:
  RedirectURL == http://docomo.ne.jp/mn/ == http://problemkaputt.de/
The TTY debug window displays higher-level I-Mode messages (and enabling JOY
logging will also show lower-lever controller messages).

PSX Games/Software for I-Mode Adaptor (Japan only)
  Sxxx-????? Doko Demo Issyo (PlayStation the Best release only) (Sony) 2000

The supported games should have the I-Mode adaptor logo on the CD cover (the
logo depicts two plugs: a PSone controller plug, and a smaller I-Mode plug).

functions.

Lightspan Online Connection CD is using a regular dial-up modem for internet
(instead of mobile I-mode phones).
"Dragon Quest Monsters 1 & 2" was announced/rumoured to support I-mode
(however, its CD cover doesn't show any I-Mode adapter logo; and the game does
reportedly require entering passwords for "manual" data transfer between PSX
and mobile phones).

The Keitai Eddy SIO cable was bundled with the Keitei Eddy CDROM. The SIO cable
was apparently discontinued and replaced by the SCPH-10180 cable because newer
PSone consoles don't have SIO ports.
Unknown if both cables were made by the same manufacturer. The newer SCPH-10180
games are NOT backwards compatible with the old SIO cable.
Keitai Eddy is an untility for editing things like ring tones, the main menu
supports dozens or hundreds of phones from different manufacturers - unknown if
it does have any "internet support", or if it's merely capable of editing phone
settings. Unknown if the Keitai Eddy cable contains a microprocessor, or if it
does merely pass-through UART signals with some small voltage protection
circuit.

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Libimode Library
-----------------------------------------------

I-Mode PSX Library
There is an offical document summarizing the I-Mode features for PSX:
http://lorezan.free.fr/ps1/iMODE.pdf Software Development Seminar: iMode System
It does include some info about a data structure and command/state values for
the libimode library:
 sceImode_Param Context Structure
  00h short fCommandType        Command type (00h..07h)
  02h short fPortNo             iMODE cable connection port (0:port1, 1:port2)
  04h short fSlotNo             iMODE cable connection slot (A~D:0~3) (unused)
  06h -     padding             -
  08h char* fSendBuff           Send data buffer address           ;\
  0Ch short fSendBuffSize       Send data buffer size              ; TX
  0Eh short fSendDataSize       Actual size of send data           ;/
  10h char* fRcvBuff            Receive data buffer address        ;\
  14h short fRcvBuffSize        Size of receive data buffer        ; RX
  16h short fRcvDataSize        Size of receive data buffer        ;/
  18h char* fInfoBuff           Info data receive buffer address   ;\
  1Ch short fInfoBuffSize       Info data receive buffer size      ; Info ?
  1Eh short fInfoDataSize       Actual size of info data received  ;/
  20h short fStatus             State variable (00h..10h)
  22h short fLastError          Error class (signed, -63h..+00h)
 Commands:
  0=IMODE_CMD_RCV               Check receive data (default)
  1=IMODE_CMD_SND               Send request
  2=IMODE_CMD_STS               Get state
  3=IMODE_CMD_ABORT             Abort send/receive
  4=IMODE_CMD_AUTH_START        Begin authentication
  5=IMODE_CMD_AUTH_END          End authentication
  6=IMODE_CMD_GW_CONNECT        Connect gateway
  7=IMODE_CMD_GW_DISCONNECT     Disconnect gateway
 States:
  -1 =UNINITIALIZED       Pre-Init / Post-Finalize
  00h=DORMANT             Initial State          ;-
  01h=AUTH_STARTING       Authenticating         ;\CND_AUTH_START
  02h=AUTH_STARTED        Authenticated          ;/
  03h=GW_CONNECTING       Gateway connecting     ;\
  04h=GW_CONNECTED        Gateway connected      ; CMD_GW_CONNECT
  05h=CONNECTING       ?  Connecting             ;/
  06h=CONNECTED        ?  Connected
  07h=SENDING          ?? Sending                ;\IMODE_CMD_SND
  08h=SENDCOMPLETE     ?? Send completed         ;/
  09h=RECEIVING        ?? Receiving              ;\IMODE_CMD_RCV
  0Ah=RECEIVECOMPLETE  ?? Receive completed      ;/
  0Bh=DISCONNECTING    ?  Disconnecting          ;\    CMD_ABORT?
  0Ch=DISCONNECTED     ?  Disconnected           ; CMD_GW_DISCONNECT
  0Dh=GW_DISCONNECTING    Gateway disconnecting  ;
  0Eh=GW_DISCONNECTED     Gateway disconnected   ;/
  0Fh=AUTH_ENDING         Authentication ending  ;\CMD_AUTH_END
  10h=AUTH_ENDED          Authentication ended   ;/

I-Mode Send requests
  req=400h   cmd=0Fh+10h       (1Fh)        ?                     ;\
  req=080h   cmd=2Fh+10h       (3Fh)        gw_connect            ;
  req=100h   cmd=43h+10h       (53h)        gw_disconnect         ; control
  req=200h   cmd=63h+10h       (73h)        ? (event 20h/21h?)    ;
  req=800h   cmd=87h+xx,n,n,n  (87h or 97h) ;5byte ;shutdown?     ;/
  req=010h   cmd=01h+xx        (01h or 11h) misc & transfer_timer ;\handshake
  req=020h   cmd=05h+xx        (05h or 15h) misc                  ; errors?
  req=040h   cmd=09h+xx        (09h or 19h) wrong_blkno_lsb       ;/
  req=00xh   event 0Ah/0Bh --> cmd=00h+xx+ttt+bbb+(Nbyte), or cmd=01h/05h+10h

I-Mode Events
  event=-1  none
  event=00h user_action_05h_11h (connect_stage_1, begin_gw_connect)   ;req=080h
  event=01h unused
  event=02h unused
  event=03h user_action_05h_12h (connect_stage_3, begin_gw_disconnect);req=100h
  event=04h unused
  event=05h trigger ;killer_xfer_req=020h      ;\generated somehow
  event=06h trigger ;killer_xfer_req=010h      ;/(send handshake error?)
  event=07h error_retry  (upon timeout, or incoming_11_01110011 error msg)
  event=08h error_giveup (after four (re-)tries)
  event=09h transfer_timer (triggers req=010h, or req=020h)
  event=0Ah    ;\send 2, 5, or N byte (send data message?) outgoing
  event=0Bh    ;/                                          outgoing
  event=0Ch    ;\                                          outgoing
  event=0Dh    ; send 2, or 5 byte (send control message?) outgoing
  event=0Eh    ;/                                          outgoing
  event=0Fh (matching blkno)     incoming_x1_bbb0nnn0_nnnnnnnn  ;\
  event=10h (wrong blkno bit1-3) incoming_x1_bbb0xxx0           ; TLP
  event=11h (matching blkno)     incoming_x1_bbb1nnn0_nnnnnnnn  ; messages
  event=12h (wrong blkno bit1-3) incoming_x1_bbb1xxx0           ;/
  event=13h   ;\                 incoming_01_bbb10001 (aka 11h) ;\
  event=14h   ;                  incoming_x1_bbb00001 (aka 01h) ;
  event=15h   ;/                 incoming_11_bbb10001 (aka 11h) ; handshake
  event=16h   ;\flags OR 10h     incoming_01_bbb10101 (aka 15h) ; errors?
  event=17h   ; result=20h       incoming_x1_bbb00101 (aka 05h) ;
  event=18h   ;/                 incoming_11_bbb10101 (aka 15h) ;
  event=19h   ;\                 incoming_01_bbb11001 (aka 19h) ;
  event=1Ah   ; flags OR 40h     incoming_x1_bbb01001 (aka 09h) ;
  event=1Bh   ;/                 incoming_11_bbb11001 (aka 19h) ;/
  event=1Ch (GW_CONNECTED)       incoming_01_01110011 (aka 73h) ;\
  event=1Dh    (req_disconnect?) incoming_x1_01100011 (aka 63h) ;
  event=1Eh   ;\                 incoming_x1_00101111 (aka 2Fh) ;
  event=1Fh   ; req=200h, and    incoming_11_00111111 (aka 3Fh) ; control
  event=20h   ; req=400h         incoming_x1_01000011 (aka 43h) ;
  event=21h   ;/                 incoming_11_01010011 (aka 53h) ;
  event=22h (GW_DISCONNECTED)    incoming_01_00011111 (aka 1Fh) ;
  event=23h (force disconnect?)  incoming_01_00001111 (aka_0Fh) ;
  event=24h (force disconnect?)  incoming_01_10010111 (aka 97h) ;
  event=25h (force disconnect?)  incoming_01_10000111 (aka 87h) ;/
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_01_bbb1nn01 (other)   ;\
  event=27h (invalid)            incoming_x1_bbb0nn01 (other)   ; handshake
  event=28h (invalid)            incoming_11_bbb1nn01 (other)   ;/
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_01_00111111 (aka 3Fh) ;\
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_11_00011111 (aka 1Fh) ; control
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_11_10010111 (aka 97h) ;
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_01_xxx1xx11 (other)   ;
  event=26h (invalid)            incoming_01_01010011 (aka 53h) ;
  event=27h (invalid)            incoming_11_00001111 (aka 0Fh) ;
  event=27h (invalid)            incoming_11_10000111 (aka 87h) ;
  event=27h (invalid)            incoming_x1_xxx0xx11 (other)   ;
  event=28h (invalid)            incoming_11_xxx1xx11 (other)   ;/

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - Unknown Features
-----------------------------------------------

I-Mode PSX software is in japanese (unknown if translations would reveal any
interesting information).
I-Mode can reportedly also send UDP messages (unknown how and what for).
I-Mode can transfer Info additionally to Data (unknown what that Info stuff is,
it seems to be related to TLP Message Type 40h/41h).
I-Mode has some monthly traffic limit (unknown what kind of status/error
messages exist).
I-Mode requires nearby radio stations (unknown what kind of status/error
messages exist).
I-Mode phones probably requires battery/chargers (unknown what kind of
status/error messages exist, unknown if it's possible to connect chargers
without removing the I-Mode data cable).
I-Mode phones should have some unique user ID or phone number (unknown what
kind of status/error messages exist; unknwn if such IDs are automatically
included in HTTP messages).
I-Mode can send emails (in PSX browser, click the option underneath of iMenu)
(unknown how the send-protocol works).
I-Mode can probably receive emails (unknown if/how the PSX browser can do such
things).
I-Mode cables can access rhe phone's address book (this is used by Keitai Eddy,
Mobile Tomodachi, and upper-right PSX browser options) (unknown how that works,
it appears to require a PIN number; the PSX seems to await a message from phone
instead of sending messages to it)).
I-Mode cables can install custom ringtones (supported by Keitai Eddy, maybe
also by PSX browser) (unknown how that works, it appears to require a PIN
number).
I-Mode phones do probably include a RTC (unknown if/how the PSX can access
that, as by now, the PSX browser's email composer seems to prompt the user to
manually enter date/time) (note: paid-for I-Mode services include Time and
Weather, but the phone should also have a RTC).
I-Mode can notify of incoming voice calls during internet browsing (unknown if
such notifications are also forwarded to PSX).
I-Mode PC-USB-cables support standard modem drivers with Hayes AT commands
(alternately to using a dedicated I-Mode driver) (unknown if that Hayes stuff
is also accessible on PSX).

Controllers - I-Mode Adaptor - References

Sony's Software Development Seminar: iMode System
